messages.body_plain:
I have a very similar issue to the OP. I have been randomly simulating data and running INLA models on it for several thousand iterations. Every 2-3 hours a situation arises that causes fmesher64.exe to keep running seemingly forever. To counter this I tried using another R functions to end the command if it took too long (i.e. got caught in the loop explained above):

mesh5<-tryCatch(evalWithTimeout({inla.mesh.2d(loc= coordinates(coords2), max.edge = c(minME, maxME), cutoff = co, offset = c(minOS, maxOS))}, timeout=60, onTimeout="warning"),error=function(e) e)

If it was stopped artificially, I then randomly changed all the inla.mesh.2d arguement values and ran the command again. This approach didn't appear work as it seem to just hang again with the different values. Would it be better to resample the input (locational) data and build a a mesh with a different number of points in this case instead?

I was also not entire sure if my approach killed the fmesher64.exe process or left orphaned programmes running?

Was this issue futher resolved?

Thanks very much.

Dave

> On Tue, 2015-10-13 at 11:44 -0700, ikam...@asu.edu wrote:
> > Currently, if someone tries to implement a quantile spatial model
> > using the asymmetric Laplace likelihood, he/she receives the
> > following message:
> >
> > Model 'laplace' in section 'likelihood' is marked as 'disabled'.
> >   Usage is not recommended and unsupported.
> >   You can enable it setting variable
> > 'enable.model.likelihood.laplace'
> >   to 'TRUE' in environment INLA:::inla.get.inlaEnv().
> >   If you chose to do so, you are on your own.
> >
> >
> > Could somebody clarify the current issues/problems related to the
> > implementation of the asymmetric Laplace likelihood?
> > In which cases can we trust the output by setting
> >  enable.model.likelihood.laplace=TRUE ?
> > Furthermore, any suggestions as to how one can alleviate the problems
> > will be appreciated.
>
> Hi,
>
> the main issue is that the double laplace has zero second deriviate of
> the log likelihood, although there is an overall 'curvature'. this
> means that there is no local information in the likelihood about the
> variance, just the mean. there are also problems with the numerical
> optimizer in this case.
>
> I doubt that laplace approximations are adequate for this case, and
> something else must be done. OR, there is some empirical evidence that
> the estimates achived are good (mean and especially the variance).
>
> For these reasons, it is disabled.
>
> It is possible to do parametric quantile regression instead, of
> course...

Dear List,
Happy new Year! (not sure how far into the new year you're supposed to keep wishing people happy new year...)

I have a (possibly) very naive question; I know that you can do a few parametric survival models in INLA, which are all characterised by the tag inla.models()$likelihood$NAME$survival=TRUE. But is it not possible to use other data models (eg Gamma), which are already implemented in INLA but have this tag set to FALSE, to run a parametric survival model? And is there any plan of potentially extending the range of parametric survival models?

Thanks
Gianluca

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] mesh generation hanging (fmesher64, inla.mesh.2d)
messages.body_plain:
My problems appear to arise from the fact that my points are sampled from (an albeit large) regular grid. Once in every couple hundred replicates a particular arrangement of points sampled from this grid cannot be turned into a mesh without hanging.

Here is my solution:

require(raster)
require(INLA)
require(R.utils)

## create random grid and sample from it - this is not my dataset so is unlikely to recreate the error
rast1<-raster()
coords2<-xyFromCell(rast1,1:ncell(rast1),spatial=T)[sample(1:ncell(rast1),20000),]

## set up error
e <- simpleError("test error")
mesh5<-NULL

### while mesh5 is not a mesh
while(!class(mesh5)[1]=="inla.mesh"){

## run mesh with time limit of 20 seconds
mesh5<-tryCatch(evalWithTimeout({inla.mesh.2d(loc= coordinates(coords2), max.edge = c(10, 100), cutoff = 0.1, offset = c(1, 25))}, timeout=20, onTimeout="warning"),error=function(e) e)
## if time limited reached tryCatch returns a simple error
if(class(mesh5)[1]=="simpleError"){

## if it fails jitter coodinates very slightly
coords2<-data.frame(x=jitter(coordinates(coords2)[,1],0.1),y=jitter(coordinates(coords2)[,2],0.1))
coordinates(coords2)<-~x+y
                   }#end of simple error if

      }## end of while

using this code you need to keep checking you running processes and manually kill any hanging fmeshers64 processes. I have written some code to identify and kill the hanging processes but it is unweidly and not annotated.

Hope this helps

Dave

On Thursday, January 14, 2016 at 11:04:00 PM UTC+11, D Redding wrote:
>
> My problems appear to arise from the fact that my points are sampled from (an albeit large) regular grid. Once in every couple hundred replicates a particular arrangement of points sampled from this grid cannot be turned into a mesh without hanging.
>
> Here is my solution:
>
> require(raster)
> require(INLA)
> require(R.utils)
>
> ## create random grid and sample from it - this is not my dataset so is unlikely to recreate the error
> rast1<-raster()
> coords2<-xyFromCell(rast1,1:ncell(rast1),spatial=T)[sample(1:ncell(rast1),20000),]
>
> ## set up error
> e <- simpleError("test error")
> mesh5<-NULL
>
> ### while mesh5 is not a mesh
> while(!class(mesh5)[1]=="inla.mesh"){
>
> ## run mesh with time limit of 20 seconds
> mesh5<-tryCatch(evalWithTimeout({inla.mesh.2d(loc= coordinates(coords2), max.edge = c(10, 100), cutoff = 0.1, offset = c(1, 25))}, timeout=20, onTimeout="warning"),error=function(e) e)
> ## if time limited reached tryCatch returns a simple error
> if(class(mesh5)[1]=="simpleError"){
>
> ## if it fails jitter coodinates very slightly
> coords2<-data.frame(x=jitter(coordinates(coords2)[,1],0.1),y=jitter(coordinates(coords2)[,2],0.1))
> coordinates(coords2)<-~x+y
>                    }#end of simple error if
>
>       }## end of while
>

messages.body_plain:
We are working on getting a version of the model into the package that would allow this, but it's not quite there yet.  In the meantime, the closest is probably to use these methods (depending on _why_ you need it it may either work or not...).
1) renormalise the model at a "base" model, so that for theta=c(0,...,0), say, the variance is constant. This can be done by changing the offset column in B.tau based on the inla.qinv output for an unnormalised model.
2) make sure you don't use a plain kappa& tau parameterisation, but instead one that is closer to decoupling the range and the marginal variances.  See for example the lindgren&rue 2015 Journal of Statistical Software paper for prototype code for that.

Finn

stack=inla.stack(data=list(y=y),
  A=list(cBind(1, B), Diagonal(length(uidx)), Diagonal(length(vidx))),
  effects=list(list(mu=1, beta=1:ncol(B)), list(u=uidx), list(v=vidx))

data=inla.stack.data(stack)
A=inla.stack.A(stack)

formula = y ~ -1 + mu + f(u, model="iid") + f(v, model="iid") + f(beta, model=?, ?)
(With whatever model you use for beta)

Note that mu and beta are confounded unless you've modified the Bspline basis to be orthogonal to a constant. But that's a general modelling issue, not specific to inla, so the solution to that problem depends on what model you really want.

Finn
